idiom_name: interface with default methods (interfaces have no instance variables)
implementation_notes: Java's interfaces may not declare instance variables, so implementing an interface adds behavior without adding a per-instance field - the empty-base concern does not arise, and the local idiom replaces the classic base-class structure. What does cost is the JVM's implementation-defined object header and field alignment: a typical 64-bit HotSpot configuration with compressed class pointers shows a 12-byte header rounded to a 16-byte object, but other JVMs, flags and compact-header modes differ. The lever is therefore the number and order of instance fields, not the base class hierarchy, and abstract base classes remain justified when subclasses need protected helpers; keep them field-free when they are intended as stateless carriers.
pitfalls: Every Java object pays an implementation-defined header, so removing a stateless interface or base does not remove that cost; on the referenced HotSpot configuration it is 12 bytes rounded to 16, but other JVMs and flags differ.
Default methods cannot read instance state and are resolved per class at load time, so an interface cannot be used as a store for shared mutable policy state.
Implementing a 'mixin' as an abstract class with a field leaks that field into every subclass and consumes the single inheritance slot, blocking other bases and mixin composition.
